Asymptomatic malaria parasitaemia in household members of confirmed malaria patients

Dataset 13: Asymptomatic malaria in households of confirmed cases in Abuja

RSR feasibility analysis

2026-08-03

Introduction

Onyiah and colleagues carried out a cross-sectional household survey in the Federal Capital Territory, Abuja, Nigeria between March and August 2016 (PLOS ONE 2018, doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0203686). Laboratory-confirmed malaria patients were recruited consecutively from twelve health facilities in three randomly selected area councils; their households were then visited within seven days and all consenting members were enrolled and screened, giving 602 participants from 107 households. Asymptomatic parasitaemia matters because people carrying parasites without symptoms are not treated, and so act as a silent reservoir that sustains transmission around a treated index case.

Aim. Among household members of confirmed malaria patients in Abuja, we examined which of age, sex, education, area council, bushes around the home, insecticidal net use, housing quality, sleeping in the same room as the index case and uncovered water receptacles are independently associated with asymptomatic malaria parasitaemia, mutually adjusting for the others.

This is a Purpose 3 analysis: several predictors are of interest and the question is which remain associated with the outcome after mutual adjustment.

Methods

Data source. A cross-sectional household survey in three of the six Abuja area councils (Abuja Municipal, Kuje, Kwali), March to August 2016. Index cases were patients with microscopy- or RDT-confirmed malaria attending twelve selected health facilities; the sampling unit for this analysis is the household member, and this teaching extract holds 602 household members with 15 variables. Because entry into the sample required living with a confirmed malaria patient, the sample is selected on exposure to a household infection and nothing here is a population prevalence estimate.

Variables. The outcome is malaria_parasitaemia, a binary indicator where the event is a positive thick-film microscopy result. There are 421 events and 181 non-events in the file, i.e. 69.9% positive. This is worth pausing on: the event is the majority class, which is unusual for a disease outcome and has a practical consequence noted under the parameter budget below. Predictors are age group (reference 20 and over), sex (reference female), highest education (reference none), area council (reference Abuja Municipal, the largest), bushes around the home (reference no), insecticidal net status (reference no net), a housing-quality index (reference improved, the largest group), sleeping in the same room as the index case (reference no) and uncovered water receptacles near the home (reference no).

Three predictors were reshaped before any model was fitted. (i) The five housing variables house_floor, house_roof, house_type, house_wall and house_window are five correlated measurements of one underlying construct, housing quality; pairwise correlations between the “improved” indicators derived from them run from 0.38 to 0.78, and the cross-tabulations contain structural zeros (every one of the 77 huts has mud walls and none has screened or glass windows; all 341 ceramic-tiled dwellings have screened or glass windows). Entered together they cost 11 parameters and generate a variance inflation factor of about 27 for house_window. They were therefore replaced by a single index counting how many of five “improved” features a dwelling has (ceramic-tiled floor, cement-plastered walls, metal or shingle roof, screened or glass windows, a dwelling other than a hut), collapsed to three levels. (ii) owns_llin and used_llin_previous_night are exactly nested: all 107 participants who used a net owned one, and all 454 non-owners are coded 0 for use, so the “did not use” category silently mixes people with no net and people with an unused net. They were combined into one three-level variable. (iii) age_group was collapsed from six levels to four, because the 20-24 stratum holds only 50 participants and the three adult strata have nearly identical parasitaemia (70.0%, 68.5% and 61.8%); the childhood strata, which are the clinically interesting ones, are kept separate.

Parameter budget. The fourteen predictors as shipped cost 27 parameters. The relevant denominator for the ten-events-per- parameter rule is not the 421 positives but the 181 negatives, because a logistic model is constrained by the smaller of the two outcome classes; the shipped set therefore runs at 6.7 per parameter, below the conventional minimum. The reduced set above costs 16 parameters, i.e. 11.3 negatives per parameter, which clears it. The budget was fixed before any model was fitted.

Statistical analysis. glm(family = binomial), justified because the outcome is binary. We fitted a univariable model for each predictor first, then a single multivariable model containing all of them. Predictors were chosen in advance on subject-matter grounds, not by significance. Coefficients are exponentiated and reported as odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals; significance threshold 0.05. Model adequacy was assessed with performance::check_model(), focusing on binned residuals, collinearity, influential observations and events per parameter, and every categorical predictor was cross-tabulated against the outcome to check for separation before fitting. The models treat the 602 participants as independent, which they are not: they sit inside 107 households, and no household identifier is shipped in this extract, so the clustering cannot be adjusted for here. The consequences are set out under Limitations. Analysis used R version 4.6.0 (2026-04-24) with tidyverse, gtsummary and performance.

Missing data. There is none. All 15 columns are 100% complete, so the complete-case analysis retains 602 of 602 rows (0 dropped) and all 421 events. This is the one respect in which the dataset is unusually easy to work with.

Positives outnumber negatives in every stratum of every predictor, which is the direct consequence of a 69.9% overall positivity rate; the informative comparisons are therefore between columns rather than within them. The clearest contrast is bushes around the home, present for 40.1% of positives against 22.7% of negatives, and education, where 24.5% of positives have no formal education against 13.3% of negatives. Net status and sleeping in the same room as the index case look almost identical in the two columns.

Parasitaemia is higher where there are bushes around the home in every age group, and the age pattern is a childhood peak at 5-9 years rather than a gradient: the school-age children in bushy compounds are the highest-prevalence cell in the figure at 89.5%.

Abbreviations: CI = Confidence Interval, OR = Odds Ratio

Bushes around the home carry the strongest crude association: their presence multiplies the odds of parasitaemia by OR 2.29 (95% CI 1.55 to 3.44) (p <0.001). Education shows a monotone crude gradient against the no-education reference — primary OR 0.58 (95% CI 0.33 to 1.01) (p = 0.056), secondary OR 0.44 (95% CI 0.25 to 0.75) (p = 0.003) and tertiary OR 0.41 (95% CI 0.23 to 0.71) (p = 0.002) — and age shows a peak rather than a gradient, with children aged 5-9 at OR 2.09 (95% CI 1.25 to 3.63) (p = 0.006) relative to adults while under-5s (OR 1.43 (95% CI 0.85 to 2.47), p = 0.189) and 10-19 year-olds (OR 1.00 (95% CI 0.65 to 1.56), p = 0.997) are not distinguishable from them. Men have OR 1.45 (95% CI 1.02 to 2.07) (p = 0.041), just inside the threshold. Intermediate housing sits at OR 0.64 (95% CI 0.43 to 0.96) (p = 0.030) but basic housing does not (OR 0.98 (95% CI 0.61 to 1.59), p = 0.927), so the housing “gradient” is not monotone and should not be read as one.

Three predictors that the study design puts front and centre are flatly null in crude analysis. Sleeping in the same room as the index case gives OR 0.78 (95% CI 0.55 to 1.10) (p = 0.159) — the point estimate is if anything protective. Owning and using a net the previous night gives OR 0.86 (95% CI 0.55 to 1.36) (p = 0.517), and owning a net but not using it gives OR 1.01 (95% CI 0.51 to 2.12) (p = 0.973), so neither ownership nor use marks lower parasitaemia. Uncovered water receptacles give OR 0.92 (95% CI 0.55 to 1.57) (p = 0.758), and neither of the two non-reference area councils differs from Abuja Municipal (Kuje OR 0.86 (95% CI 0.58 to 1.27), p = 0.435; Kwali OR 0.69 (95% CI 0.36 to 1.39), p = 0.286).

Why adjustment is needed

Area council confounds the housing and bushes associations. The three councils differ sharply in dwelling stock: only 3.1% of Abuja Municipal participants live in basic housing against 50.6% in Kuje, and bushes around the home are reported by 29.6% of Abuja Municipal households against 47.7% in Kuje. Area council is also plausibly related to the outcome independently of either, because the councils differ in transmission intensity, vector density and distance to care. Without adjustment, a housing coefficient is partly a geography coefficient.

Age confounds the education association, and severely. Education in a household survey is largely an age marker for children: of the 203 participants under ten, 198 are recorded as having no education or primary education only and the remaining 5 as secondary; not one is recorded as tertiary, whereas 48.3% of the adults are. The low-education strata are therefore dominated by exactly the young children who have the highest parasitaemia for immunological reasons. Age is independently related to the outcome through acquired immunity, and it is related to recorded education by construction. The crude education gradient therefore cannot be read as an effect of schooling or of the socioeconomic position it proxies until age is held constant.

The model carries 16 parameters. On the usual count that is 26.3 events per parameter, comfortably clear of ten, but that number flatters the model: because the event is the majority class the binding constraint is the 181 negatives, giving 11.3 per parameter. AIC falls only from 738.2 for the intercept-only model to 722.6, a drop of 15.5, and Tjur’s R-squared is 0.076. The nine predictors together explain very little: with 69.9% of everybody positive, the model has limited room to discriminate.

Among participants of the same sex, education, area council, housing, net status, room-sharing and water storage, bushes around the home remain associated with OR 2.25 (95% CI 1.46 to 3.54) (p <0.001) — essentially unchanged from the crude estimate and the only predictor significant at 0.05 with a wide margin. Among participants alike on everything else, children aged 5-9 have OR 2.18 (95% CI 1.04 to 4.66) (p = 0.042) relative to adults, while under-5s (OR 1.01 (95% CI 0.47 to 2.15)) and 10-19 year-olds (OR 1.04 (95% CI 0.61 to 1.78)) are indistinguishable from adults. Education retains a gradient after adjustment: tertiary OR 0.43 (95% CI 0.19 to 0.93) (p = 0.035) and primary OR 0.47 (95% CI 0.24 to 0.92) (p = 0.030) against no education, though secondary (OR 0.53 (95% CI 0.26 to 1.07), p = 0.081) is not significant and the levels are not ordered as a clean dose-response.

The three design-relevant exposures stay null. Sleeping in the same room as the index case gives OR 0.81 (95% CI 0.55 to 1.18) (p = 0.266); using a net the previous night gives OR 1.00 (95% CI 0.62 to 1.64) (p = 0.993), and owning an unused net OR 1.29 (95% CI 0.55 to 3.24) (p = 0.569). Housing quality (OR 0.70 (95% CI 0.45 to 1.08) for intermediate, OR 0.92 (95% CI 0.48 to 1.75) for basic) and uncovered water receptacles (OR 0.69 (95% CI 0.39 to 1.25)) are also null. These are associations among the participants observed, not effects of intervening.

The coefficient that moves furthest is age under 5, from OR 1.43 (95% CI 0.85 to 2.47) crude to OR 1.01 (95% CI 0.47 to 2.15) adjusted — the whole of the apparent excess in the youngest children disappears, moving all the way to the null. This is the education entanglement described above operating in reverse: under-5s are almost all in the “no education” reference stratum, so once education is in the model the “no education” coefficient absorbs the childhood excess and nothing is left for age to carry. Fitting the same model without education returns the under-5 estimate to 1.52, close to its crude value, which confirms the mechanism. Area council moves in the opposite direction, away from the null: Kuje goes from OR 0.86 (95% CI 0.58 to 1.27) to OR 0.62 (95% CI 0.38 to 1.03). Crudely Kuje looks like Abuja Municipal, but Kuje households have far poorer housing and lower education, both of which are associated with more parasitaemia; hold those constant and a lower Kuje odds emerges. This is classic masking rather than confounding away a real signal. Uncovered water receptacles move the same way, from OR 0.92 (95% CI 0.55 to 1.57) to OR 0.69 (95% CI 0.39 to 1.25), though null in both columns.

Two coefficients barely move. Bushes goes from OR 2.29 (95% CI 1.55 to 3.44) to OR 2.25 (95% CI 1.46 to 3.54), a shift of a few percent, so its association is essentially independent of everything else measured; and tertiary education goes from OR 0.41 (95% CI 0.23 to 0.71) to OR 0.43 (95% CI 0.19 to 0.93).

Three contrasts change significance, all in the same direction — losing it. Sex goes from p = 0.041 to p = 0.060, crossing 0.05 with almost no change in the point estimate (OR 1.45 (95% CI 1.02 to 2.07) to OR 1.43 (95% CI 0.99 to 2.10)), which is a loss of precision rather than confounding. Secondary education goes from OR 0.44 (95% CI 0.25 to 0.75) (p = 0.003) to OR 0.53 (95% CI 0.26 to 1.07) (p = 0.081), attenuating toward the null because secondary-educated participants are disproportionately adolescents and young adults, so age adjustment removes part of the crude contrast. Intermediate housing goes from OR 0.64 (95% CI 0.43 to 0.96) (p = 0.030) to OR 0.70 (95% CI 0.45 to 1.08) (p = 0.108), confounded by area council as anticipated. Nothing becomes significant on adjustment.

Diagnostics

Separation. No shipped predictor separates the outcome on its own: every one of the 14 variables has both a positive and a negative in every level, so Zero cells is 0 throughout. The smallest cell anywhere is 3 observations, in house_type at level “bungalow”, which has only 3 negatives among 25 participants. In the fitted model no coefficient is extreme: the largest absolute log-odds is 0.85, the largest standard error is 0.46, and fitted probabilities span 0.36 to 0.96, nowhere near 0 or 1. There is no separation in this model. Sparse combinations are a different matter and are documented in the feasibility notes.

Collinearity. All variance inflation factors are modest once the housing variables have been reduced to an index: the largest is 3.94 for educ, and because most of these are multi-level factors the fairer figure is the standard- error inflation factor, whose maximum across all nine terms is 1.26. The five raw housing variables entered together would have given a VIF near 27 for house_window; the index removes that entirely.

Binned residuals. Only 84% of binned residuals lie inside their error bounds, against a target of 95% or more, so the model is imperfectly calibrated. With so few negatives spread across 602 observations each bin contains only a handful of them, which makes the check noisy, but the shortfall is real and should be reported rather than waved away.

Influence. No observation dominates: the largest Cook’s distance is 0.016 and the largest leverage is 0.097, both far below any conventional threshold. This is expected in a dataset with no continuous predictors and no rare categories.

What does not apply. Homogeneity of variance and normality of residuals are assumptions of the linear model, not of logistic regression, and the panels check_model() produces for them are not interpreted here.

Discussion

Among household members of confirmed malaria patients in Abuja, 69.9% carried malaria parasites without symptoms, and almost nothing measured in this survey distinguishes those who did from those who did not. The one robust finding is that having bushes around the home is associated with roughly 2.3-fold higher odds of parasitaemia, an association that is essentially unchanged by adjustment for age, sex, education, geography, housing quality, net use and room sharing. Children aged 5-9 also stand out, at OR 2.18 (95% CI 1.04 to 4.66) relative to adults. Practically, this points at peridomestic vector breeding habitat and at school-age children as the targets for reactive case detection around a treated index case.

The negative findings are as important as the positive one. Sleeping in the same room as the index case — the exposure the study design exists to measure — shows no association at all (OR 0.81 (95% CI 0.55 to 1.18)), and neither owning nor using an insecticidal net the previous night is associated with lower parasitaemia (OR 1.00 (95% CI 0.62 to 1.64) for use). With a positivity rate of 69.9% across the whole sample, infection is close to universal in these compounds, and a within-household exposure contrast has very little variation left to explain.

Limitations. The most serious problem is clustering. The 602 participants come from 107 households, an average of about 5.6 people each, and household members share the same compound, the same vector exposure, the same bushes, the same roof and the same index case. Every standard error and p-value above assumes they are independent, which they plainly are not, so the confidence intervals are too narrow and the p-values too small — most acutely for the household-level variables (bushes, housing, area council, water receptacles), which really have at most 107 independent values, not 602. No household identifier is shipped in this extract, so this cannot be corrected here; the published analysis used generalised estimating equations with the household code as the clustering variable, which is not reproducible from these columns. The quantitative size of the problem is estimated in the feasibility notes.

The sample is selected on household exposure: everybody here lives with a laboratory-confirmed malaria patient, so 69.9% must not be quoted as a prevalence for Abuja or for Nigeria, and the null net and room-sharing associations may reflect a ceiling effect in a very high-transmission subset rather than genuine absence of effect. The design is cross-sectional, so reverse causation is live for the modifiable exposures: households that have recently had a malaria case may have acquired or started using nets in response, which would bias the net association toward or past the null. Exposure measurement is crude — bushes around the home, uncovered water receptacles and net use the previous night are single self-reported or observed-once items, and net use says nothing about how the net was used or whether it was still insecticidal. The housing index is a construction, not a validated instrument; it weights five features equally and its middle category is not intermediate in risk, so its coefficients should be read as descriptive. Education is substantively invalid for a large part of the sample: 203 participants are under ten and 29 under-fives are recorded as having primary education, so the variable is partly an age marker and partly noise, and its coefficients cannot be given a schooling interpretation. The binned-residual check fails. Unmeasured confounders that matter here — indoor residual spraying, recent antimalarial treatment, altitude and proximity to standing water, whether the index case was still parasitaemic — are simply not in the file. All estimates are associations, not causal effects.

Future work. Refit with the household identifier as a clustering variable, using either generalised estimating equations or a household random intercept, and add parasite density so that low-density carriage can be distinguished from clinically meaningful infection.

Final reduced model (this document) 16 0 0.8 0.5 0.9637582 no
  • MAJOR (structural, and the dominant problem): the 602 participants sit in 107 households and no household identifier is shipped. Household sizes run from 1 to 20 with a mean of 5.6. Recovering the household code from the source supporting file (see the chunk above; students cannot do this) gives an intraclass correlation of 0.28 on the latent scale from an empty random-intercept model — household variance 1.25 against the logistic residual variance of 3.29 — and it stays at 0.26 after adjustment for all nine predictors, so the covariates explain almost none of the household-level variation. At a mean cluster size of 5.6 that is a design effect of about 2.3: the effective sample size is roughly 265 participants, not 602, and the effective number of negatives is about 80, which turns the model’s 11.3 negatives per parameter into about 5.0. On the same fitted model, cluster-robust standard errors are a median of 1.10 times the naive ones overall, but the split is the instructive part: a median of 1.24 for the household-level predictors (worst: housingIntermediate (3-4) at 1.53) against 1.09 for individual-level ones, and one individual-level term (sexMale) actually gets smaller. In all, 3 coefficients cross 0.05 when the clustering is respected: age_grp5-9 and educPrimary lose significance and sexMale gains it. A household random intercept inflates the standard errors further still (bushesYes from 0.226 to 0.336). Recommendation: ship household_id in the CSV. It is one integer column, it is present in the source file, the published paper’s own analysis depends on it, and without it a student cannot do anything about the single largest methodological problem in the dataset. If it stays out, the caution needs to say plainly that the clustering cannot be corrected, not merely that a simple model “does not account for” it.
  • MAJOR: selection on exposure. Every participant lives with a laboratory-confirmed malaria patient. The 69.9% positivity is a within-outbreak-household figure and must never be quoted as a population prevalence. It also compresses the exposure contrasts: with seven in ten positive, same_room_as_index_case, owns_llin and used_llin_previous_night have almost no discriminating room left, which is the likeliest explanation for all three being null.
  • MAJOR: the outcome is the majority class, 421 positive versus 181 negative. Students who count “events” as the 1s will compute 26.3 events per parameter and conclude they can afford a large model; the binding constraint is the 181 negatives (11.3 per parameter here, and only about 5.0 once clustering is allowed for). The full fourteen-predictor set costs 27 parameters, i.e. 6.7 negatives per parameter, which is over-fitting. Worth flagging in the brief because every other logistic dataset in this catalogue has a minority-class event.
  • MAJOR: the five house_* variables are one construct with structural zeros. house_type and house_wall are nearly aliased (all 77 huts have mud walls; all 55 bungalows and duplexes have cement-plastered walls), and all 341 ceramic-tiled dwellings have screened or glass windows. Entered together they give house_window a VIF of about 27 and house_type about 9 while adding almost nothing: the crude positivity rates across the three levels of the composite index are 72.2%, 63.0%, 72.6% respectively, i.e. non-monotone and essentially flat. Housing quality simply does not predict this outcome, so the choice between the five raw variables and a composite changes nothing substantive — but the five raw variables will produce nonsense-looking coefficients that a student then has to explain.
  • MAJOR: age_group * education separates completely. The interaction is the obvious thing to reach for once someone notices the education gradient is age-driven, and it fails hard: 3 terms are aliased (no under-5 has secondary or tertiary education, no 5-9 year-old has tertiary), the largest surviving interaction coefficient is 16.2 on the log-odds scale with a standard error of 1455.4, and the largest fitted probability is 0.9999998. An interaction between two of the housing variables does the same: house_window * house_wall produces a coefficient of 14.7 with a standard error of 441.4, because only 4 participants have cement-plastered walls and open windows and all 4 of them are positive. That single four-person cell is the specific culprit. house_type * area_council does not diverge but aliases 4 terms, because duplexes occur only in Abuja Municipal and huts only in Kuje and Kwali.
  • MAJOR, and easy to miss: R issues no separation warning in any of these models. The 0/1 fitted warning column in the stress-test table reads “no” throughout, including for age_group * education, because glm() only warns when a fitted probability exceeds 1 - 1e-8 and the largest here is 0.9999998 — just under the trigger. A student who treats “no warning” as “no separation” will report a coefficient of 16.2 with a standard error of 1455.4 as a finding. The reliable detectors here are the standard errors, the aliased NA coefficients and the cross-tabulations, not the warning.
  • MAJOR: owns_llin and used_llin_previous_night are exactly nested. All 107 users are owners; all 454 non-owners are coded 0 for use. Putting both in a model does not separate — the model runs — but the “did not use” reference then pools 454 people with no net and 41 people with an unused net, the two coefficients become uninterpretable mirror images (in the full shipped model they are 0.29 and -0.29 on the log-odds scale, cancelling almost exactly), and each carries a variance inflation factor above 4.5. The three-level recode used here is the only coherent parameterisation.
  • MINOR but worth knowing: education is fully observed and substantively meaningless for a third of the sample. There is no missingness to warn about — which is itself the trap, because nothing flags the problem. 91 participants are under five, of whom 29 are recorded as having primary education, and 5 children under ten are recorded as secondary. The variable is an age proxy below age ten and an SES proxy above it, and the two age groups it entangles are the ones with the highest parasitaemia. Concretely, adding educ to the model moves the under-5 odds ratio from 1.52 to 1.01 — the childhood signal is transferred wholesale to the education term.
  • MINOR: area_council is thin at one level. Kwali holds only 41 participants (15 negatives), so its confidence interval is wide (OR 0.58 (95% CI 0.23 to 1.41)), and Kwali contains no roof-shingle dwellings at all, which is part of why the raw housing variables behave badly alongside it. Three levels is still workable; two would not be an unreasonable collapse.
  • MINOR: house_type = bungalow is the sparsest single cell, with 3 negatives out of 25 participants (88.0% positive), and house_window = metal_shutters has only 11 participants in total. Neither produces separation on its own, but both are one dropped observation away from it.
  • MINOR: binned residuals fail (84% inside the bounds against a 95% target). With 181 negatives spread over 602 rows the check is genuinely noisy, but a student following the diagnostics honestly will have to report a failed check and should not be penalised for it.
  • MINOR: the outcome is test-dependent, and the source file shows the tests disagree. The supporting file carries both a microscopy result and an RDT result for every participant. Microscopy gives 421 positives; the RDT gives 83, the two agree on only 39.9% of participants, and Cohen’s kappa is 0.07 — no better than chance. Only the microscopy result is shipped, which is defensible (it is the result the paper’s headline figure uses), but it means the 69.9% figure is a property of one assay, not a robust fact about the households.
  • Not a problem: missing data. All 15 columns are 100% complete, so the complete-case sample is the full 602 rows with all 421 events. There is no listwise-deletion story to tell here at all, which makes this a good dataset for teaching everything except missing data.
  • Not a problem: model stability. The final nine-predictor model has a maximum standard error of 0.46, a maximum Cook’s distance of 0.016, a maximum leverage of 0.097 and fitted probabilities confined to 0.36-0.96. Nothing is unstable; the trouble with this dataset is conceptual, not numerical.
  • Overall verdict: usable, with warnings. The outcome supports a real Purpose 3 analysis with a defensible reduced predictor set, and it produces one clear finding (bushes), one clear age pattern and a set of instructive nulls. But Tjur’s R-squared is only 0.076 and the AIC gain over the null model is 15.5, so students should be warned in advance that a well-executed analysis here will find very little, and that the interesting write-up is about why.
